cues.text: Why does a nanomaterial behave differently from the same material in bulk?
A bulk material is anything we can see and feel: powdery, granular or lumpy. Even a millimeter powder is still bulk.
Grind it into microparticles. You can no longer see them one by one, but their properties barely change.
Only around one hundred nanometers do the properties really start to change.
The reason is the surface.
Cut a cube into smaller cubes. The volume stays the same, but the surface keeps growing. Nanomaterials have a very high surface area to volume ratio, in square meters per cubic meter.
Now look at the atoms. In a cluster of nine hundred and twenty-three atoms, thirty-nine percent sit on the surface.
Three hundred and nine atoms: fifty-two percent. Fifty-five atoms: seventy-six percent.
And in a cluster of thirteen atoms, ninety-two percent of the atoms are on the surface.
So at the nano scale, surface-related properties begin to dominate over bulk properties.
Almost every property changes. The exam wants each category with its example.
Physical: melting point. Chemical: reactivity. Electrical: conductivity. Mechanical: strength. Optical: light emission.
And the trap he warned about: reactivity is chemical, not physical. The physical example is the melting point.
Start with a chemical property: catalytic activity. It depends on the size and the shape of the particle.
A reaction has to climb an energy hill, the activation energy. Catalytic activity is inversely proportional to it.
Smaller particles need less activation energy, so they are more active. They are better catalysts.
That matters for petroleum processing, energy conversion and removing pollutants. You do not need a new catalyst. Use the same one, in nano size.
Take the melting point, a physical property.
Atoms melt when they have enough energy to overcome the forces holding them in fixed positions.
An atom inside is held by neighbours on every side. A surface atom touches fewer atoms. It has unsaturated bonds.
So surface atoms need less energy to move, and they melt first.
A nanoparticle is mostly surface, so it melts at a lower temperature than the bulk material.
Three more categories.
Electrical: bulk carbon conducts the same whatever its size or twist. A carbon nanotube changes its conductivity with its cross-section, and when it is twisted.
Nano wires stay conductive even when they are tiny, and that keeps computer chips shrinking.
Optical: bulk gold is yellow, but nano gold is red, because its electrons are not free to move as in bulk gold.
Biological: nanoparticles pass biological barriers, such as the cell membrane and the blood-brain barrier. The lecturer called this the most important application.
Finally, a definition he called very important. Learn it word for word.
A nanomaterial is a material with at least one dimension in the nano size regime: one to one hundred nanometers.
Why not up to one thousand? At five hundred or nine hundred nanometers, the material still behaves like bulk.
Surface atoms start to dominate only below about one hundred nanometers. That is where nano begins.
